Defined benefit

 

There’s a silver lining to rising interest rates and soaring borrowing costs: Corporate pension funds have finally rebounded after years of deep deficits.

 

When the bond market gets tough and yields rise sharply, it can be easy to focus on the losers. But higher rates produce winners, too. For companies that still operate old-fashioned pension plans, higher yields mean higher discount rates, which are key to calculating the present value of their liabilities.

 

So while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the Federal Reserve and plenty of bond investors are anxiously watching each tick higher in long-term yields, S&P 500 pension plans are healthier than they’ve been in almost two decades.

 

They finished slightly overfunded last year, with plan assets equivalent to 103% of pension obligations, according to Zion Research Group. That was the highest ratio since 2007, after which they were underfunded for 16 years straight, bottoming at about 77% funded in 2012.

 

Even as interest rates climbed sharply off their pandemic lows, returns on assets have been solid, especially publicly traded equities. At the same time, the projected benefit obligation for the S&P 500 shrank to about $1.4 trillion at the end of 2025 from $2.3 trillion five years earlier.

 

The single biggest driver was a $553 billion actuarial gain, meaning the present value of promises owed to employees had declined. This was mainly because of higher discount rates, even as the plans paid out $517 billion in benefits. Some companies have taken advantage of the windfall by executing pension-risk transfers, shifting obligations to life insurers through annuity buyouts.

 

Companies disclose their pensions’ funded status typically only once a year. But early indicators point to continued improvement. The discount rate used for the FTSE Pension Liability Index was 6.12% at the end of August, up from 5.61% at the end of last year. That signals corporate pension liabilities are still contracting.

 

Meanwhile, Zion estimates plan assets this year returned 3.9% through Aug. 31. That is based on benchmark index performances and assumes an asset mix that is almost half fixed-income, with the rest mainly in public equities and alternatives.

 

While that return might not seem impressive, what matters is it is positive while obligations are falling. In other words, assets are outperforming liabilities.

 

Milliman, an actuarial consulting firm, tracks the funded status of the 100 largest corporate defined-benefit plans. Its latest monthly report showed the funded-status ratio was about 112% as of July 31, up from 106% at year-end.

 

The catch is that if interest rates decline, discount rates will drop, pushing the present value of liabilities back up.

 

For now, though, it’s worth remembering that in markets, one side’s pain is another’s gain. Even if Chicken Little is right and the sky is falling, somewhere out there a roofer is about to enjoy a record quarter.

The excitement surrounding Moderna and Merck’s personalized mRNA cancer vaccine added more than $50 billion in combined market value for the two drug companies. But it is also creating a gold rush in a growing corner of healthcare: tumor sequencing.

 

Personalized cancer therapies require a genetic roadmap for each patient. The tumor has to be sequenced to identify the mutations the vaccine should target. If these therapies become blockbusters, the diagnostic companies doing that sequencing could hold a lucrative tollbooth on every dose.
